entry.title: How did pinwheel calculators work?
entry.content:
As a handful of readers might know, I am a bit of a calculator nerd. I’m especially fond of mechanical four-function calculators that had their heyday between the 1920s and 1960s and then disappeared without a trace.

A video is worth a thousand tokens, so to explore the ingenuity of these designs, let’s start with a short clip of a Vaucanson calculator from my collection:

In the first half of the video, I demonstrate addition. I calculate 1234 + 4321 by placing the first operand in the input register (top), turning the crank clockwise to add this value to the accumulator (bottom right), and then entering the second operand and cranking again. To subtract from the stored value, I’d instead turn the crank counterclockwise.

The second and more interesting half shows multiplication: I solve 79 × 123 by entering the first operand and then turning the crank three times to load 79 × 3 into the accumulator. Next, I shift the accumulator carriage one decimal digit to the right and crank twice; because the accumulator is offset from the input register, this has the same effect as cranking twenty times in the original position; in other words, I add 79 × 20. Finally, I shift the carriage once more and complete one more turn to add 79 × 100. Note that the crank counter in the bottom left now reads “123”, confirming that we multiplied the first operand by the correct value.

To divide, I’d load the first operand into the accumulator and then successively subtract power-of-ten multiples of the second number. This would give me the integer result in the counter register and the remainder in the accumulator.

Alright — so how does this work? Well, if you pop open a pinwheel calculator, you will be greeted by a pretty complicated mechanism:

There’s a lot going on here, but the most important part of the assembly is the cylindrical stack of input disks, one per digit, as seen in the top right of the photo. Each disk has three main components: a center section mounted to a keyed shaft that stays in position until the main crank is turned; a set of nine radial pins that slide into grooves in that disk; and a freely-moving digit-setting ring with a track and a couple of detent positions:

Each pin has a protrusion that rides in the track of the digit-setting ring. By turning the input lever one way or the other, we can change the number of pins that extend from the assembly.

When the crank is turned, the entire assembly rotates and these extended pins mesh to an intermediate gear that advances the digit at the corresponding position of the accumulator:

Of course, this mechanism is not enough: without a way to carry to the next column, 0001 + 0009 would give us 0000 instead of 0010. To implement carry, each input disk (except for the rightmost one) is also equipped with a spring-loaded carry pin. This pin sticks out at all times, but is normally out of the path of the intermediate gear — offset to the right — so it has no effect on the output value.

To actually perform carry, each digit of the accumulator is equipped with a cam that shoves a wedge-shaped carry-sensing lever into the path of the carry pin just as the value rolls over from 9 to 0. This wedge in turn deflects the carry pin to the left, momentarily placing it in the path of the intermediate gear for the next decimal digit.

This is a mouthful; the entire process is shown in the following video:

The carry-sensing lever is pushed back into the home position before the drum completes a full rotation, thus resetting the mechanism.

Note that the carry pins are staggered and do not engage at all once; this is to allow carry to effortlessly ripple through all digits if necessary (e.g., when adding 9999 + 1).

There’s a couple of additional convenience and reliability features in each pinwheel calculator; this includes interlocks to prevent out-of-sequence inputs, as well as reset levers for each register. There’s even a mechanical bell on overflow or underflow. I won’t bore you with all the gory details, in part because these mechanisms are less interesting — but if you’re morbidly curious, this ancient YouTube video provides a more complete walkthrough.

And if you want to learn about the prehistory of calculators, I invite you to check out my 2023 article:

PS. Yep, this is why one of the registers on all Intel CPUs, used as the implicit destination for some opcodes, is called the “accumulator”.

I write articles about electronics, math, philosophy, and more. If you like what you see, please subscribe.

entry.title: I checked Clojure's core with Lean and found unreported bugs
entry.content:
I checked Clojure's core with Lean and differential testing and found unreported bugs in HAMT and vector-of

I read Koukyosyumei's article "èåãªRustè£½OSSãLean 4ã§å½¢å¼æ¤è¨¼ãã¦ã¿ããããã¡ããã¡ããã°ãè¦ã¤ãã£ãè©±" (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs"). The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain. Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples. I checked the collections with differential testing against the java.util collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org. They include reduce on vector-of, the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries. The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as = and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21. The links to the source point to the clojure-1.12.7 tag.

How I checked

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition. You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32, the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations. So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of %.

When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code. I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property. Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results. For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

For vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level. The operations were conj, pop, assoc, and their transient versions.

I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before. I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

reduce on vector-of never finishes

vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays. Clojure implements it in gvec.clj, written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector. If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

(reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65504)))) ;; => 2145354256 (reduce + (drop 1 (into (vector-of :long) (range 65505)))) ;; => never returns (reduce + (drop 1 (vec (range 65505)))) ;; => 2145419760

The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj, where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

(recur result (bit-and 0xffe0 (+ aidx 32)))

The code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it. With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504. After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce. In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position a that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at a + 32.

import Std.Tactic.BVDecide def stepImpl (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := 0xffe0 &&& (a + 32) def stepFix (a : BitVec 64) : BitVec 64 := (~~~0x1f) &&& (a + 32) theorem impl_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) : stepImpl a = a + 32 := by unfold stepImpl; bv_decide theorem fix_ok (a : BitVec 64) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0) : stepFix a = a + 32 := by unfold stepFix; bv_decide

impl_ok fails with the counterexample a = 1073741792, and #eval stepImpl 65504 returns 0 as well. fix_ok uses (bit-not 0x1f) as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that a is a multiple of 32 below 0x7fffffe0.

dissoc on a HAMT collision node hides another key

Clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree. Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a HashCollisionNode at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with =.

HashCollisionNode.without builds the new node with one key removed. It should give the new node its own hash, this.hash, but it passes the parameter hash instead.

return new HashCollisionNode(null, hash, count - 1, removePair(array, idx/2));

The parameter hash is the hash of the key you pass to dissoc. If you dissoc with a key that is = to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.

In Clojure, a vector is = to a Java ArrayList with the same elements, but the two hash differently. CLJ-1372 tracks this mismatch.

In the example below, I chose a and b so that both ArrayList keys hash to 1003.

(def a (java.util.ArrayList. [0 42])) (def b (java.util.ArrayList. [1 11])) [(hash a) (hash b) (hash [0 42]) (= a [0 42])] ;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true] (def m3 (-> (hash-map a :A b :B) (dissoc [0 42]) (assoc a :A2))) [m3 (count m3) (get m3 b)] ;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil]

When you print m3, you can see the key b, but (get m3 b) returns nil. After the dissoc, the node records 1867155179, the hash of [0 42]. The next assoc then concludes that a, with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.

A lookup of b follows the branch for 1003 and finds only a there, so it never reaches b. In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to dissoc needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.

disj on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient dissoc! does not.

I changed that line in the 1.12.7 PersistentHashMap.java to this.hash and compiled it. With the patched class ahead of the jar on the classpath, the same example returned :B for (get m3 b).

removeIf gives different results with and without a type hint

Since Clojure 1.12, you can pass a Clojure function directly where a Java method takes a functional interface. CLJ-2864 removed the logic that read the function's return value as a Clojure truthy value.

In prior alphas, the FI adapter returns inserted Clojure truthy return logic when adapting a Clojure function to an FI with boolean return.

The compiler follows this for calls where it knows the type. A call without a type hint goes through reflection and uses Reflector.coerceAdapterReturn. That method still applies RT.booleanCast to a boolean return value, so the same .removeIf call gives a different result depending on the type hint.

(let [l (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3])] (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l)) ;; => ClassCastException (let [l (identity (java.util.ArrayList. [1 2 3]))] (.removeIf l #{1 2}) (vec l)) ;; => [3]

Wrapping the list in identity hides the type of l, so the call goes through reflection.

A set used as a function returns the element itself. In the call with a known type, the adapter cannot turn the Long into a Boolean and throws. The reflective call reads the return value as true and removes the elements.

int overflow and a negative subvec index

Clojure 1.12 added IDrop implementations that make drop faster. The ones for string seqs and vector seqs add the current position and n as ints and then compare the sum with the length. StringSeq.drop for string seqs is one of them.

(drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (next (seq "abc"))) ;; => StringIndexOutOfBoundsException Index -2147483648 (drop Integer/MAX_VALUE (seq "abc")) ;; => ()

The Lean model gave the counterexample i = 2147483646 and n = 2147483647. I changed the check to compare n with the remaining length s.length() - i. Under the assumptions 0 < i < s.length()= and 0 < n, Lean proved that the fixed check matches the naive specification for every 32-bit input.

For assoc on the result of subvec, SubVector.assocN does not reject a negative index.

(assoc [2 3] -1 :x) ;; => IndexOutOfBoundsException (let [s (assoc (subvec [0 1 2 3 4] 2 4) -1 :x)] [s (.-v s)]) ;; => [[2 3] [0 :x 2 3 4]]

The call overwrites an element of the underlying vector outside the subvec, and returns a subvec that looks unchanged. CLJ-962 fixed the same bug in nth, but assoc still has it.

Other findings

The other 12 bugs have a smaller impact, and I reproduced each of them on Clojure 1.12.7.

Behavior Example reduce-kv throws on vector-of (reduce-kv f [] (vector-of :long 5 6)) With a functional interface of three or more arguments, a call with a known type truncates an int return value without an error (fn [a b c] 4294967297) returns 1, and (fn [a b] 4294967297) throws ArithmeticException next on a seq of a string, a primitive array, or an infinite repeat keeps the metadata (meta (rest (with-meta (seq "abc") {:m 1}))) is {:m 1}, and for a vector's seq it is nil (long ##NaN) and (int ##NaN) return 0 (long ##NaN) is 0, and (byte ##NaN) throws long clamps a double 2^63, and int a float 2^31, to the maximum value (long (Math/pow 2 63)) is Long/MAX_VALUE char wraps a BigInt at 2^64 (char 18446744073709551681N) is \A float rejects ##Inf but lets ##NaN through (float ##Inf) throws, and (float ##NaN) is ##NaN Boxed and primitive doubles use different range checks when converted to byte and similar types (byte (identity 127.9)) is 127, and (byte 127.9) throws get truncates a fractional index on strings and Java arrays (get "abc" 1.9) is \b byte-array and short-array reject an initial value (byte-array 2 7) throws On a seq of a primitive array, .indexOf and .contains disagree (.indexOf (seq (byte-array [1 2 3])) 2) is -1 .lastIndexOf on a list compares with equals instead of = (.lastIndexOf (list 1 2) (int 2)) is -1
Where I found nothing

PersistentHashMap and PersistentHashSet matched java.util.HashMap over 3 million operations that mixed persistent and transient updates. The tests also covered maps before an update staying unchanged, ArrayNode splits and merges, and collision nodes down to depth 7.

PersistentTreeMap matched java.util.TreeMap and kept the red-black tree invariants. Vectors matched ArrayList around every tree boundary I tested.

On the numeric side, Lean proved for 64 bits that the check Numbers uses to pick the fast path for addition and subtraction agrees with the overflow check.

For multiplication, bv_decide timed out at 16 bits, so I checked 8 and 10 bits. I proved up to 32 bits that clojure.core/mod matches the floored remainder.

Every property I proved in Lean holds for the model shown in this article. I checked that each model means the same thing as the Java code by comparing it with the source and with the reproduced behavior.

entry.title: A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond
entry.content:
One night earlier this fall, a biologist and YouTuber in Florida named Joseph Ricketts went snorkeling in a retention pond next to his local Home Depot.

A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond

He found it teeming with life and beauty.

He filmed what he saw and posted a video to his channel titled “Night Snorkel In a Home Depot Retention Pond.” It quickly blew up, hitting more than 2 million views as of this writing, and for good reason: It’s not at all what you might expect.

Ricketts found an aquatic world teeming with life on his dive into what is, from the surface, a stagnant pool of water filled with old beer cans. A water snake undulated through the pond, a bulge in its stomach revealing a recent meal. Tadpoles darted about, some of them half on their way to froghood. Mysterious shrimp scuttled along the silty bottom.

Ricketts, who works as a crocodile and alligator research biologist in Florida, went for his first snorkeling trip when he was 16 years old. On that trip, he came face-to-face with a manatee — and was instantly hooked. “I experienced so much joy in that moment, and I just kind of subconsciously knew I’d be chasing that for the rest of my life to some degree or another,” he told me.

Ricketts still takes a lot of joy in snorkeling, in part because of how it allows him to quickly access a totally different world hiding just under the surface of the water; his YouTube bio declares, “I’ll snorkel pretty much anywhere.” And his recent retention pond dive among the suburban detritus bears that out.

I talked with Ricketts recently about urban ecology, snorkeling, and what motivates a person to jump into the pond behind the Home Depot three miles from his house (his shortest-ever commute to a dive yet). Our interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Why snorkeling?

That’s a good question. I’m scuba certified, and I enjoy anything underwater, but snorkeling is just super accessible. I have a camera housing and a wet suit and other gear, but really all you need is just a mask and snorkel. As long as the water’s not freezing cold, you can get in there and take a look around. I really enjoy how, as soon as you immerse your head, it feels like you’re in a totally different world.

But the beautiful thing is that you’re not. You’re in the same world, it’s just this is the one that you didn’t have a vision into before. It’s kind of a meditative, calming practice. Just taking a look around at what is happening in nature and how things survive in their own environment is pretty awesome. I love it.

Okay, but why this pond?

I honestly had the idea for it a couple years ago. I’d see people out there birding with binoculars and telephoto lenses, and I started wondering if I could snorkel in there. We’ve had a drought so I couldn’t do it for a really long time, and when we finally got some rain I decided to go for it.

Tell me about the retention pond. What is it — and why is it in this Home Depot parking lot?

Florida has a lot of low-level, very wet natural ecosystems, but it’s also an extremely developed state. There are strip malls and roads and concrete everywhere! Natural wetland environments can soak up intense stormwater, but when you totally change environments and put in shopping centers and neighborhoods and pave everything with asphalt, you kind of lose that ability. That stormwater needs a place to go and collect — or it’s just going to flood parking lots and stores and houses.

So they have to put these retention ponds in; nowadays, you can’t build in certain areas unless you put in a retention pond. Not far from the Home Depot is a new-build neighborhood, and they have a retention pond that they had to put in, but they set it up with a little walkway for people that live in the neighborhood. That’s nice because there’s some wildlife that’s able to survive and live there, and people can enjoy this sort-of natural area. But it’s also not as good as the original thing that may have been there, you know?

So you were snorkeling in what’s essentially a replacement for a wetland that might once have been there.

I don’t know the history of that area exactly, but I imagine there was some form of wetland.

What was the most surprising thing that you found?

One thing that I found was a tadpole shrimp, which people call triops. It’s a freshwater crustacean that apparently is not native to Florida. When I saw it underwater, I had no context for what it is. As a biologist, people assume you just know wildlife, but people forget how much wildlife there is in the world! I know a lot about alligators and crocodiles, but there’s still a ton I don’t know. I think it’s important to sometimes be able to be like: “I don’t know what I’m seeing or why I’m seeing it” — and then hopefully I can learn about it.

But anyway, I saw this thing, I had no clue what it was, and I asked a bunch of my coworkers about it but they had no clue what it was either. So then I had to do some research online, which is how I finally figured it out.

“I think that was kind of a personal challenge I had for myself: Can I see something beautiful in a retention pond?”

Apparently they are native to the Midwest. They lay their eggs in soil, and then during times of rain, they really quickly hatch and feed and grow, and then they reproduce, lay more eggs, and then wait for the next cycle while it’s dry. It’s a real quick boom-and-bust life cycle. It’s not a native species, but I think there’s just a couple areas in this state where you can find them — and one just happens to be right there in the retention pond.

I saw that there were also more common animals there, like frogs, snakes, and dragonflies. But how do you think they all got into this parking-lot pond?

A lot of frog species adapt to urban environments and find any bit of water they can. They were probably used to a forest and wetland, and now they’ve had to adapt to what’s available currently, which is pretty limited.

I think that’s true for most of the animals you find in there. The natural world is pretty resilient, though sometimes I think we give it too much credit for how resilient it can be.

What do you mean by that?

Life survives, but the way things originally were does not necessarily survive, and I think that’s something that’s really worth protecting. The way some people interpreted the video was like: ”Wow, look at all this life persisting even in this place!” And it was amazing and there is beauty there, but you can’t just accept that and then get rid of all our natural wetlands. We need untouched, expansive ecosystems.

It can be cool to be excited about this little retention pond and what lives in here, but coupled with that also needs to be excitement for protecting huge untouched habitat as well. Both are full of worthy things.

Do you think the retention pond, now that it’s there, is worth preserving?

I think so. One thing I didn’t really get to dive into with the video too much is the idea of a nature desert. I don’t know if I’m making that term up, but it’s kind of related like a food desert: Depending on your demographic or where you’re born, that might be the only bit of nature you have access to. It’s a privilege to be able to travel to a national park or a big state park or something, and not everyone has that opportunity. Your only exposure to nature could be a retention pond that’s in the middle of a city somewhere. And so I do think those places are very worth protecting, because I think it’s important that regardless of your background, if you’re a kid, you have a place that you can go to and feel safe and be exposed to wilderness even if it’s very small urban wilderness.

Do you think people should be snorkeling in more retention ponds?

[Laughs] I don’t recommend that people do that! There are some retention ponds where you could encounter some nasty stuff.

It was definitely a little bit of a stunt. But I also want to help people think about ecological ideas that they might not otherwise think of, while still enjoying the watch.

Another thing I want to get at is so many people responded like: “That’s gross, how could you do that?” But my question is why are we just totally okay with having these huge bodies of water that are gross and contaminated in our everyday lives? Clean water should be the norm!

Still, it’s a place that should be valued and thought of differently.

Do you feel like your own perception of urban ecology or urban environments changed after this?

I think so. That’s another reason why I love snorkeling: I feel like somehow each time I do it, it changes me a little bit. I didn’t know that much life was out there, and I didn’t know what a lot of those creatures were when I first got in. It deepens my personal connection with my local Home Depot in a way I hadn’t really thought would happen five years ago, but here we are.

Do you think you’ll do more urban snorkeling? I know you just went to the Dry Tortugas, which is a very different environment from Home Depot.

I think I am going to look into it. I’m not going to become the retention pond snorkeling guy; I hope to diversify my snorkeling more than that. But I definitely think this is an idea that resonates with people, and it gives me an opportunity to explore some interesting ecological and even philosophical concepts.

I’ve got some other ideas that I’ve been waiting for the right time to film. There’s a place up in the Carolinas that’s a Frisbee golf course with a little creek running through it, and there are these amazing minnow spawning events that happen in the creek, so maybe one day I’ll be out there in the creek filming minnow spawning while people are playing Frisbee golf nearby.

What are you hoping people take away from the video?

One thing that I hope people take away from a lot of my videos is just a sense of wonder at what’s out there in the natural world, and maybe a broader definition of beauty. I think beauty can be found in unexpected places and from unexpected creatures. I think that was kind of a personal challenge I had for myself: Can I see something beautiful in a retention pond? And do I have the skill with my camera to present that so that maybe other people catch a little glimmer of it too? And I think it happened, which is really exciting.

But at the same time, I hope people realize how important it is that big expansive habitats are protected and conserved too, and that it’s not just about the big animals like polar bears and manatees, which are kind of easy to care about, but also little rare invertebrates or spiders or snakes, all of which I believe have inherent value and are worth protecting.

entry.title: Deriving Black-Scholes
entry.content:
Deriving Black-ScholesOption price from the no-arbitrage hypothesis.

Even if it feels unintuitive, the price of an option does not depend on whether you expect the underlying to moon or tank. Under some reasonable market hypotheses, we can build a fully hedged portfolio by holding the underlying and shorting the option. Since it is riskless, by no-arbitrage assumption, it must return the same as the risk-free interest rate. That allows to put together an equation (the Black-Scholes equation), and solve for the option price (the Black-Scholes formula).

Model §

A European call gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy an underlying at a fixed price \(K\!\), the strike, on a fixed date \(T\!\), the maturity. Its value \(V\!\) is the premium you need to pay for having that optionality, and it depends on time and on the underlying stock price \(S\!\). At maturity it is the payoff1 1 For example, pay $5 today for the right to buy one AMZN share for $200 in a month. If AMZN then trades at $230, you buy at $200 and the option is worth $30. If it trades at $180, you walk away and the option is worth nothing.

\[V(T,S)=\max(S-K,0).\]

Stock moves scale with price, so it is common to model the returns instead of the price. Over a short time the return is a small drift plus noise. The noise is the sum of many small, unpredictable2 2 Weak-form efficient market hypothesis: past prices do not predict future moves. sources. Such sum can be modeled as a Brownian motion \(W\!\),3 3 By the central limit theorem, the sum of many small independent variables is normal. so the return is

\[\frac{dS}{S}=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW\!,\]

with drift \(\mu\) and volatility \(\sigma\!\). For our model, we will assume constant drift, volatility and interest rate \(r\!\). We will also assume “perfect” trading, with fractional shares allowed, no fees, no taxes, no dividends, and no arbitrage.

Hedged portfolio §

The trick of Black-Scholes is to build a fully hedged portfolio combining the option and the underlying in the right proportion. By the no-arbitrage hypothesis, its returns must be the same as the interest rate \(r\!\), and that way we can put together an equation.

When the stock moves a little, the option moves by \(\Delta\) times as much, with

\[\Delta=\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}.\]

If you short one option and hold \(\Delta\) shares, then the two moves cancel. This is a delta hedge.

Note that \(\Delta\) changes with the stock price and time. The portfolio is riskless only over an instant, and stays so only if it is rebalanced continuously.

Black-Scholes equation §

Use the Taylor expansion of the option value and keep the terms up to order \(dt\). Since \((dW)^2=dt\), the \((dS)^2\) term is one of them,

\[dV=\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}dt+\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}dS +\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}(dS)^2.\]

Substituting the stock model gives

\[dV=\left(\mu S\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}+\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} +\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}\right)dt +\sigma S\frac{\partial V}{\partial S}\,dW.\]

Now, we can use the same hedged portfolio \(\Pi\) as before, short one option and long \(\Delta\) shares, which is worth \(-V+\Delta S\!\). Holding \(\Delta\) fixed over an instant,

\[d\Pi=-dV+\Delta dS,\]

and substituting \(dS\) and \(dV\!\) gives

\[d\Pi=\left(-\frac{\partial V}{\partial t} -\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}\right)dt.\]

See how noise and drift cancel. No \(dW\!\) term is left, and everything else is known at time \(t\), so over the next instant the portfolio change is fixed.4 4 A known return with no randomness is precisely what riskless means. We’ve built a riskless portfolio, that by the no-arbitrage assumption, it must earn the risk-free rate, \(d\Pi=r\Pi\,dt.\) Equating both expressions gives us the Black-Scholes equation

\[\frac{\partial V}{\partial t}+rS\frac{\partial V}{\partial S} +\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2S^2\frac{\partial^2V}{\partial S^2}=rV.\]

Note that \(\mu\) is gone, so the option price does not depend on the drift.

Black-Scholes formula §

I won’t bore you with the technical details,5 5 For the details, see John C. Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, 11th edition, Pearson, 2021. The Bible of derivatives. but the above equation can be solved by a change of variables to turn it into the heat equation, whose solution is known. Define

\[\tau=T-t,\quad x=\ln S+\left(r-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\tau,\quad V(t,S)=e^{-r\tau}w(\tau,x),\]

where \(w\) is the option value at maturity. Substituting, all terms but two cancel, and we get the heat equation

\[\frac{\partial w}{\partial\tau}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\frac{\partial^2w}{\partial x^2}.\]

With the payoff as initial condition, the solution is

\[w(\tau,x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2\tau}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \max(e^y-K,0)\,\exp\left(-\frac{(y-x)^2}{2\sigma^2\tau}\right)dy.\]

Completing the squares gives the Black-Scholes formula

\[V(t,S)=S\,N(d_1)-Ke^{-r\tau}N(d_2),\]

where \(N\) is the standard normal CDF and

\[d_1=\frac{\ln(S/K)+\left(r+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt{\tau}}, \qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{\tau}.\]

\(N(d_1)\) is the hedge ratio \(\Delta\), so the first term represents the price of an asset-or-nothing call, which pays the share if the call ends in the money.\(N(d_2)\) is the risk-neutral probability of exercise, so the second term is the present value of the expected strike payment.

That’s all, lads, go make Ken Griffin broke.

entry.title: 1Password Security Incident
entry.content:
Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.

by 1Password

November 25, 2026 - 4 min

Related Categories What happened

On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.

What information was affected

The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:

Names and email addresses

Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times

Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)

Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)

Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery

Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)

The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.

When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.

What was not affected

Your vaults and the items in them

The keys that protect your vaults

1Password does not store your account password or secret key

Account recovery keys

1Password apps and browser extensions

 What we’ve done

Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.

Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.

Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.

Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.

Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.

 What you can do

Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.

1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.

Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.

If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.

 Our commitment to you

You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.

We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

entry.title: The polynomial Hirsch conjecture is false [pdf]
Holy shit holy shit holy shit holy shit: The magnitude of what’s now happening
entry.content:
HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT

I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.

Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.

There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log27) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.

Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that!

But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N)1/2+o(1). The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!). All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered, rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.

To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE—that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.

It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.

All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next. It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.

I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.

For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden. Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between. Just please don’t deny what’s happening. Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean certificates, don’t be a raging doofus who seizes on some triviality (e.g., a minor discrepancy between the Lean and informal proofs, or unused sections of the Lean proof) to pretend that dozens of great open problems of math and theoretical computer science are not, in fact, getting solved. Because they are getting solved. It might take us years to understand the solutions, but my working assumption by this point is that any proof that comes directly from OpenAI or Anthropic is correct barring information to the contrary.

I can’t possibly put the matter better than one of my friends on Facebook:

After years of crackpot “solutions” claiming Millennium Problems are solved, now that we have actual solutions, we have crackpot “refutations” claiming Millennium Problems are not solved. It is really poetic, in a way.

Along the way to so many lower bounds that we wondered whether ever we’d live to see, there will also, of course, be further shocking upper bounds: that is, ultimate barriers to lower bounds, also known as “algorithms.” And yes, some of those algorithms will break currently deployed cryptosystems.

Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area. However, until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells. I do not wish to be responsible for spreading unverified rumors. And I worry that exact statements of what was done may have been mangled in a game of Telephone.

I also, crucially, don’t want the cryptography part of the story to overshadow the intellectual enormity of what’s happening. If, in these days of long-prophesied revelation and wonders and terrors, your main worry is your Bitcoin wallet, then go somewhere else for rumors about whether or not ECDSA is broken or whatever. I don’t have what you’re looking for here.

Let me be clear: for those of my readers who celebrate, I believe that tomorrow would be a superb Thanksgiving to spend some quality time with your kids and parents and siblings and old friends.

Right now—this past week—is very much like I would’ve always imagined the beginning of an AI singularity to look and feel like. I just hope we’ll get lucky, and it will “merely” be a singularity for our little corner of the world that involves hard math problems.

At some point at dinner last night, Dana had a sneezing fit. So I said to her, I hope it isn’t a swarm of nanobots that’s come to infect us! But if it is, then I hope it’s the friendly kind, the kind that will usher us all into an AI utopia.

Now, of course, another morning has dawned, and we’re still here. May we find a world where we and our children will be happy to live at the bottom of this rollercoaster. May we work to make it so.

Nevertheless, remote corruption vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel are the kind of thing where I expect updates to be available within hours, not days or weeks. entry.title: The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
entry.content:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”

The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features

An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’

Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.

It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”

In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.

It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.

Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

entry.title: Much shorter version of GRH Lean verification from Anthropic
entry.content:
Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.

A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude (https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude.

grh/: readable edition, about 300,000 lines. Start at grh/GUIDE.md. grh-compact/: the same five theorems, about 76,000 lines.

Each folder is its own Lake project with its own README.

Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder:

lake exe cache get lake build lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean

A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing).

The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it.

entry.title: Deploying a payphone on a tiny Pacific Island for fun and zero profit
entry.content:
For the past few years Australia’s Telstra has run a campaign of “Free calls to Santa” from the universal service obligation funded payphones across the country – It’s a really fun idea and we wanted to replicate it on our network on Norfolk Island where we run the mobile network, but the’s no payphones.*

* There is now a payphone – You probably already guessed this.

Getting a Payphone to a small island in the South Pacific

Step 1 was getting a payphone.

Those who have seen my office / shed / studio / the HackHouse, know that I may have one or two payphones… But this needed a payphone that could stand the elements and be modern ish.

The answer, is of course, to use the sexiest payphone of all time; the Nortel Millennium. Featuring VFD display, durable keypad, card service, coin service, no fancy metering line required.

Unfortunately Nortel’s bankruptcy in 2008 meant I couldn’t phone up an account manager, but with the hookup of some guy with a U-Haul van full of Millennium’s in the US and a bit of a road trip, Cody from our team managed to pickup some really clean GTE branded payphones for the job.

Then Cody flew to Sydney where we drove to the house of someone who was heading to Norfolk the next day to explain they’d need to leave all their baggage at home as all of their baggage allowance was to be taken up with the weight of a payphone – Thanks Paul.

Programming

Eventually with the Payphone on Norfolk, we needed to get it programmed; for that there’s Howard Harte’s great mm_manager, which, with the aid of a USB modem is able to program the phones.

Sidebar: I also got this working with a softmodem (A fork of D-Modem with some minor tweaks I’ve documented here), so we could do it via straight SIP without the USB modem required – but the USB modem was the easier path.

The Philtel blog post covers how to setup your Millennium if you’re looking to play along at home yourself.

I hit a bit of a stumbling block with mm_manager as the software assumed you were part of the North American Numbering Plan (NANP) – as one of the literally dozens of people who live outside of America, having to put a 1 in front of the number wasn’t going to fly.

After some trial and error I sussed out what bits on the config files that get pushed to the phone controls this and submitted a PR to mm_manager which is now merged.

We’re also able to set the messaging that appears on the screen, which I’m very happy with the branding on.

We set it for free-on-net calls, so anyone can call any Norfone number without charge and the Payphone tag number.

Talking to Santa

Once this would’ve been the hard part, I did some work a long time ago with IBM Watson and built some stuff to annoy voters via phone with automated phone calls and capture their human responses and sort them and play the appropriate response. But tech has come a long way since 2019, and this was the easy part of the project.

We setup the payphone to make HOHOHO (464646) a destination that did not require coins when we did the rating table setup when programming the phone.

The ATA the payphone is connected to just comes through to our IMS like any other fixed line subscriber; the TAS is setup to zero-rate the destination and then it’s dialplan forwards it to “Santa Bridge” listening for SIP on port 5090.

I’ve got 4 pre-recorded “Norfolk Specific” greetings to buy us time to get everything setup in the background, once these greetings play (each ends asking the caller their name) then we feed into the OpenAI API.

One of the members from our team attempted to ask Santa to write a Python script to iterate over a for loop, while another team member asked Santa for firearms. In both cases it did a good job of redirecting.

All the code for this is on Github.

Branding

The phone came GTE branded, so we needed to redo the card with the branding on it that goes around the screen. Two screws and some wiggling later we pulled out the card, and then I badgered my partner into using their day off to design a new one, with a retro style I really like.

Installation

The install was beautifully completed by long-time-reader-of-the-blog Minas from Shield Electrical and Air.

He knocked up a housing to Shield it from the rain and elements and installed it outside the office entrance.

Getting it on Payphone Tag

The last step of the puzzle was making the phone so it could be captured by cult game Payphone Tag – I reached out to Alex and gave him the info, and now it’s there in the map for anyone to capture.

Future payphone adventures

So with this now in place, we’ve still got to give it some tinsel and Christmas cheer, and I’ll get some more pics of it in place.

We’re waiting for someone to claim it on Payphone tag, and we’ve shipped 3 of these to another even more remote Island I’ll hopefully be able to share more info on later.

If you’re ever on Norfolk, give it a call.

entry.title: Bare Metal Qwen
entry.content:
A standalone bootable x86-64 operating system that runs Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B directly on hardware or KVM with no Linux, no Windows, no C, no Rust, and no libc.

24,252 bytes stripped static Multiboot 1 kernel (FAST_Q8=1, default: .text = 17,143 B, .rodata = 2,772 B, .bss = 2.1 MiB NOBITS, zero dynamic dependencies), or 23,612 bytes (FAST_Q8=0, legacy Q8_0xFP32). 74–94 ms cold boot to interactive asm-llm> multi-turn chat with persistent KV-cache across turns, all SMP cores online, and the .asmbin v2 (614 MiB FP16 scales) or v1 (649 MiB FP32 scales) model bound zero-copy from physical RAM on 2 MiB huge pages. 100% token-exact and byte-for-byte parity with Phase 1 across 1..32 vCPUs. 134.9 tok/s decode on QEMU KVM (AMD EPYC 7642, 16 vCPUs; 23.7 tok/s at 1 vCPU, 118.1 tok/s at 8 vCPUs, 136.6 tok/s peak) and 55.4 tok/s live on a 0 GB disk Proxmox VE VM (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 12 cores).

Running live on a diskless (0 GB storage) Proxmox VE VM booted from the hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO (Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 12 cores, 2 GiB RAM):

x86-64 CPU with AVX2 + FMA + F16C. Core build & QEMU KVM: sudo apt install nasm binutils qemu-system-x86 Optional, for building a bootable BIOS+UEFI hybrid ISO (make os-iso): sudo apt install grub-pc-bin grub-efi-amd64-bin grub-common mtools xorriso An exported models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin file (--scale-dtype fp16 v2 recommended, or legacy v1 --scale-dtype fp32; see Phase 1 setup).

From the repository root (FAST_Q8=1 is enabled by default; pass FAST_Q8=0 for legacy FP32-activation mode):

make os FAST_Q8=1 make os-check

Expected output (FAST_Q8=1):

-rwxr-xr-x 1 user user 24252 build/asm-llm-os.elf build/asm-llm-os.elf: ELF 32-bit LSB executable, Intel 80386, version 1 (SYSV), statically linked, stripped There is no dynamic section in this file.

(The kernel is linked as 64-bit ELF and wrapped into ELF32 via objcopy -O elf32-i386 for standard Multiboot 1 loaders like QEMU -kernel and GRUB2; boot.asm transitions immediately into 64-bit Long Mode.)

Boot directly in the terminal over COM1 serial (-nographic):

qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \ -kernel build/asm-llm-os.elf \ -initrd models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin \ -nographic

Or use the Makefile shortcut:

make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16

Run a one-shot batch prompt with clean ACPI shutdown:

make os-run MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin SMP=16 \ CMDLINE='prompt="Explain how a CPU cache works in 3 concise sentences." max_tokens=64 think=0 shutdown=1'

Open a live 80x25 VGA GUI window with PS/2 keyboard input:

qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \ -kernel build/asm-llm-os.elf \ -initrd models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin \ -vga std -serial stdio

Packages the 23 KB kernel, GRUB2 Multiboot 1 config, and the 649 MiB .asmbin model into a single self-contained ~661 MiB bootable ISO (build/asm-llm-os.iso):

make os-iso MODEL=models/qwen3-0.6b-q8_0.asmbin

Boot the ISO in QEMU KVM (SeaBIOS or UEFI OVMF):

# Legacy BIOS (SeaBIOS) qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \ -cdrom build/asm-llm-os.iso -nographic # UEFI (OVMF) qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -cpu host -m 2G -smp 16 \ -bios /usr/share/ovmf/OVMF.fd \ -cdrom build/asm-llm-os.iso -nographic

Because the entire OS and model live inside the ISO and run out of RAM, the VM needs zero hard disks.

Upload build/asm-llm-os.iso to your Proxmox node's ISO storage (local -> ISO Images -> Upload, or scp into /var/lib/vz/template/iso/asm-llm-os.iso). Create and start a diskless VM on the Proxmox host (pick an unused <vmid>, e.g. 250): qm create 250 \ --name asm-llm-os \ --machine pc \ --bios seabios \ --cpu host \ --cores 12 \ --memory 2048 \ --balloon 0 \ --vga std \ --serial0 socket \ --ide2 local:iso/asm-llm-os.iso,media=cdrom \ --boot order=ide2 qm start 250 Interact either through the Proxmox web UI (noVNC Console, VGA + PS/2 keyboard) or over the virtual serial port: qm terminal 250

(Note: --cpu host is required so the VM exposes AVX2 + FMA, and --balloon 0 ensures 2 GiB of contiguous guest RAM for the 649 MiB model + 449 MiB KV-cache arena.)

By default, the bare-metal console runs in multi-turn chat mode with persistent KV-cache: each new user turn prefills only the new Qwen3 chat tokens starting at g_chat_pos without recomputing earlier turns, closes every assistant turn in the KV-cache with <|im_end|>\n, and displays live context usage (ctx=X/2048) in the decode stats line. When the KV-cache approaches max_seq (pos + n_prompt + 64 >= max_seq), it prints [chat] context full, resetting KV-cache and resets cleanly. If booted with prompt="..." and shutdown=0, the initial batch turn stays in the KV-cache so you can continue the same conversation in the REPL.

Both PS/2 keyboard (VGA) and COM1 serial (115200 8N1) are polled simultaneously. Type any message and press Enter, or use a built-in command:

Command Action /clear, /new, /reset Clear conversation history (g_chat_pos = 0, prints ctx=0/2048) /think Enable Qwen3 <think>...</think> reasoning mode /nothink Disable reasoning mode (direct answers, default) /bench Reset KV-cache and run built-in latency/throughput benchmark prompt /halt or /quit Trigger clean ACPI S5 poweroff /help Show available console commands

entry.title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again
Minipg: PostgreSQL as a Single Executable
entry.content:
minipg is PostgreSQL as one executable, ready to use, with no server to configure. A .pgdb directory is the database: its data, config, credentials, and Postgres version all live inside it, and minipg app.pgdb opens a psql shell on it. A server starts when a command needs one and stops on its own when it's idle.

minipg embeds Docker Hub's postgres:18-alpine image and runs it with h9, used as a Zig library. h9's Linux personality runs Alpine's own Postgres binaries directly on the host's hypervisor, with h9's Plan 9 kernel answering their system calls. There's no Linux kernel to boot, no VM image, and no Docker.

The demo downloads about 35 MB. It needs JavaScript Promise Integration, which Chrome and Edge have from version 137; other browsers are getting it. It can also be opened on its own page.

The demo runs minipg's Linux build, which runs inside the Postgres image itself. It starts Postgres as ordinary processes and serves on a unix socket, since a page has no TCP. New databases come from a template cluster made at build time, because initdb takes half a minute on v86.

minipg app.pgdb # psql shell (creates app.pgdb if missing) minipg app.pgdb "select 1" # one statement minipg url app.pgdb # postgres://postgres:...@127.0.0.1:54321/app minipg serve app.pgdb # an explicit foreground server minipg run app.pgdb -- npm start # your app, with DATABASE_URL set minipg dump app.pgdb > dump.sql # and minipg restore app.pgdb dump.sql

A .pgdb holds minipg.toml (settings and the generated superuser password) and pgdata/, Postgres's data directory as plain files. A stopped one can be copied like any directory. New clusters use Postgres's builtin C.UTF-8 locale, which sorts the same on every platform.

In CI, the Linux binary is static and needs no privileges or devices: without /dev/kvm, h9 runs Postgres on its native backend. A test job can be as small as:

minipg init test.pgdb minipg run test.pgdb -- go test ./...

The README lists every command, and the manual is the full guide.

Exactly one process runs Postgres for a .pgdb, enforced by a lock. It holds the server's h9 machine, whose Linux root is the unpacked image and whose writable working directory is the .pgdb. The image's docker-entrypoint.sh initializes the cluster on first start. Commands never host Postgres themselves. If no server is running, they start one in the background and use it. psql, pg_dump, and the other tools each run in their own short-lived h9 machine (about 90 ms to start) over the same root.

Linux x86_64 KVM, or h9's native backend without it (Linux 5.11 or later) Linux arm64 KVM macOS (Apple Silicon) Hypervisor.framework The browser h9's web host, v86, and minipg's Linux build

The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Building needs Zig 0.16, plus curl, jq, tar, and xz for the root:

git clone --recursive https://github.com/progrium/minipg cd minipg make build # pulls the root for this host's arch, builds ./minipg make root ARCH=386 make web # this page's demo, in .zig-out/web

minipg is early, and h9's Linux personality is young. On h9's native backend, Postgres is about 2x slower than native for one client, and slower under load. Don't trust it with data you can't recreate yet.

Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.
